title: “How Do You Remember What You Read?”: Helpful Practices for Improving Our Recall of Professional Reading r-recall-of-professional-reading/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart answers the question of how he remembers his professional reading by rejecting the idea of a photographic memory and building on Dan Willingham's principle that we remember what we think about. He proposes that teachers cultivate intellectual urgency through practices that make them think hard about what they read. These include naming burning questions before choosing a book, protecting a daily reading time, selecting books carefully and often by author rather than topic, following footnotes and citations, and giving up the goal of simply finishing books. He argues the aim of professional reading is retaining knowledge that improves teaching, not completion. The post is a practical professional-development guide to reading for retention, with a brief mention of connections between texts and writing about reading as further practices.
points: Memory for reading is not a talent but a by-product of thinking hard about the material, so build conditions that force that thinking.
Start from burning questions about your classroom or school and pick books to answer them, with a protected daily reading slot.
Choose books by trusted author and recommendations, and learn the basic principles of learning so you can sort wheat from chaff.
Follow footnotes and prioritize reading indelibly over reading quickly or finishing.
quotes: The good news is that both the science of learning and the wisdom of the ages disagree with this common assumption, and the bulk of the evidence favors the idea that there are certain practical processes by which the human mind remembers things in a way that it is able to later recall.

This is an inescapable truth about the human creature, and one that provides all kinds of practical ramifications. But for our purposes today, the takeaway is clear: one of the simplest methods for ensuring we remember our professional reading is cultivating the conditions that make energetic thinking about that reading a matter of course.
The best way to be sure that you’ll think about what you read is by making sure that you’ve got to know more about X, Y, or Z.

This is a serious matter, for I think that these questions only burn so long until the problems that they stem from overwhelm the fire and so extinguish it. Even if it’s fifteen minutes per day, it is critical to sit in one’s reading chair with that pile of books in pursuit of an urgent question.

Many books sold at teacher’s conferences are nothing more than the thoughts of the authors. While some of these thoughts are good and wise, many others simply seem good and wise while actually being superficial replications of whatever is presently vogue. These latter types of books have led many astray.

I find it to be true that I more frequently make progress on my burning questions by way of reading deeply or widely of a single (and excellent) author than I do by searching on Amazon for a title that best fits my question.
Making our main goal as readers the completion of a book is like making our main goal as teachers the retirement from teaching. It’s a way of wishing one’s life away and missing the point.
